extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic and philosophy; readers learning/analyzing syllogistic and inductive reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria for correct syllogistic and inductive reasoning (classification of propositions, proper formulation of premises, and limits of formal devices such as numeric quantification or predicate-quantification). Useful for assessing logical arguments and pedagogy in classical logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish definition from factual premise
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition (or part of a definition) differs from a statement of fact: definitions are not falsifiable in the same way factual assertions are. In a syllogism one premise may be a definition (true as definition) while another is a factual statement (which may be false).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing properties to imaginary entities you must mark that the attribute is 'imagined' (e.g., change 'A dragon breathes flame' to 'A dragon is imagined as breathing flame'), otherwise you implicitly assert reality. In analyzing syllogisms check whether a premise is a definitional clause or an empirical claim; conflating the two can mask that the real (false) premise is the factual one, not the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obversion and equivalent propositional forms
rubrics_metrics.description: One common class of equivalent transformations is obversion — changing from affirming a proposition to denying its negative (or vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use obversion as a legitimate immediate inference (as Mr. Bain terms it). Recognize standard equivalent propositional forms when testing arguments for validity or converting forms for syllogistic treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion of particular negative forms (Hamilton's observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some A is not B may be converted into the form No B is 'some' A (e.g., 'Some men are not negroes' -> 'No negroes are some men').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to awkwardness or counterintuitive surface readings when converting particular negatives; these conversions can be formally correct but may yield unintuitive phrasings that require interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of oppositions (contraries, subtraries, contradictories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositional oppositions are classified as Contraries (All A is B / No A is B), Subtraries (Some A is B / Some A is not B), Contradictories (All A is B / Some A is not B; No A is B / Some A is B), and relations of subalternation (All A is B & No A is B; Some A is B & Some A is not B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating argument forms, identify which opposition relations hold between premises and potential conclusions, since these relations determine permissible immediate inferences and where contradictions or incompatibilities arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of singular propositions in syllogisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether singular propositions (e.g., 'Socrates is wise') should be classed with universals/totals in syllogistic reasoning is contested. One view treats singulars as mere abbreviations yielding no real inference; another allows singular syllogisms where premises are independent factual claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess singular-syllogism cases by asking whether predicates are merely connoted by the proper name (in which case there is no real inference) or whether the predicates are independent factual attributes. Beware treating mere grammatical abbreviation (joining premises into one statement and then omitting a part) as a genuine inference; such 'inferences' may only reproduce less than was already stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerically definite propositions and inference (De Morgan)
rubrics_metrics.description: If premises state numerical proportions (e.g., percentages or counts like 'most Bs are C' quantified as 60% etc.), then one can derive definite minimal overlaps (e.g., a lower bound for As which are Cs) by arithmetic combination of the proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate 'most' and similar qualifiers into explicit proportions when available to obtain precise conclusions (e.g., 60% and 70% premises imply at least 30% intersection). But note the author’s practical critique: ordinary reasoning rarely supplies the numerical precision required, so the calculi of numerically definite syllogisms have limited practical utility outside specially quantified cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantification of the predicate (Hamilton's proposal) — formal availability vs psychological fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantifying the predicate (e.g., reading 'All A is B' as 'All A is some B' or 'No A is any B') yields a revised set of syllogistic rules and can amplify the legitimate moods and make figures less essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This device is valuable as a formal test — any ordinary-form proposition can be rephrased with predicate-quantification and judged by Hamilton's rules. However, be cautious: quantifying the predicate may not reflect what is in the speaker’s mind (it may be an artificial linguistic maneuver) and can lead the analyst away from the mental content of the proposition; evaluate whether the technical rephrasing aids or obscures the intended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom for deduction: 'Nota notæ est nota rei ipsius' vs dictum de omni
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed axiom ('the mark of a mark is a mark of the thing itself') is presented as a better foundational principle for deductive inference than the usual dictum de omni ('what is true of a class is true of every thing included in the class').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this axiom to highlight the condition that makes application of a general principle a real inference. But also observe legitimate objections: it may fail to account for partial coincidence (A carries B but other things also carry B), so when transferring attributes through a middle term, explicitly make the necessary limitations rather than assuming coextensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for partial coincidence when transferring attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: When A 'carries' B and B 'carries' C, it is not safe to infer that A 'carries' C without limiting for the fact that other things also carry B or C; failure to account for such limitations yields mistaken co-extensional inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the informal error of inferring reciprocity (that because A carries B, B carries A). Use conversion rules and explicit warnings about non-reciprocity; in practice, ensure the transfer of attributes accounts for other carriers of the intermediate attribute and explicitly state any limiting conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major and minor premises as precautions, not necessities
rubrics_metrics.description: Major and minor premises in the syllogistic form are not logically necessary for reasoning itself but serve as safeguards to prevent erroneous inference by specifying the kind of likeness required between cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating reasoning, recognize that the real inferential work often rests on implicit comparisons of particulars; the syllogistic major and minor formalize these comparisons to prevent error. Expect that informal reasoning may omit formal major/minor formulations; require them when precision or avoidance of mistake is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express general propositions to reflect inductive inference ('Any man is mortal')
rubrics_metrics.description: General propositions used in inductive reasoning better express their role if phrased as 'Any man is mortal' (inference from particulars A, B, C to other particulars) rather than the usual 'All men are mortal', because the former shows the general proposition vouches for particular-to-particular inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When framing or evaluating inductive arguments prefer formulations that make explicit the inferential role of the generalization (it vouches for extending observed likenesses to new particulars). This helps avoid the misleading impression that the general statement itself is the proof of the particular rather than a device summarizing the evidential basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating exact likeness with strict identity of attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat the attribute of 'man' in different individuals as a numerically distinct attribute just because the sensations or manifestations differ; general terms denote the common resemblance (a single attribute in the general sense), not many distinct attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating concepts and their role in inference, maintain the notion of the 'One in the Many' — general names denote a common resemblance across instances. Reject views that fragment general concepts into distinct per-instance attributes, since that undermines general language and general knowledge.
